top.line: Readers pay for what they read, after seeing value
top.para: On 10 October, in seven releases between 12:09 and 15:49, the sgit.ai reading meter became a working pay-on-demand publication. Readers pay pence for the share they read, from a balance that never blocks, and a rating sets the price from free to double. Once a Stripe link is set, the only question is whether people pay.

s0.line: Seven releases built pay-after-reading without planning the end
s0.para: Seven releases in 3 hours 40 minutes added a meter, depth pricing with no block below zero, personas, versions, sharing and a price-setting rating. Reading stays in the browser. Each feature grew from using the last, the ILC zigzag at work, every decision started from the reader, and the missing piece is traffic.

features.line: Depth pricing, a never-blocking balance and personas you own
features.para: A new article costs 10p and an older one 5p, charged for the share read. Everyone starts with £5.00 and can go below zero with no wall, topping up through one £5 Stripe link. A card rates usefulness, setting the price from free to double, and personas build newsrooms kept in the browser.

after.line: Paying after seeing value has mixed but useful evidence
after.para: Leanpub lets readers choose a price before reading; the card reverses that. Pay-what-you-want raised photo purchases from 0.5% to 8.39% (Gneezy, 2010), though some buy less, so the card starts at the price. Blendle's refunds reached 50% for gossip before it dropped pay-per-article, and only 17% pay for online news.

reader-first.line: Never rip off the reader; aim for value
reader-first.para: Charging the maximum makes customers feel something is expensive, so they use and recommend it less. The sweet spot is value for money. The draconian "Don't charge me" button gave way to a rating, so readers who saw no value do not pay, which also measures the journalism page by page.

how.line: Each feature grew from using the one before
how.para: From a Portuguese newsroom wallet, the meter went live at 13:40, personas came at 14:23, versions at 14:29, sharing at 15:28 and the reader card at 15:49. Designing the end state up front would have over-engineered it. The Wardley map shows each new component resting on boring ones already built.

ilc.line: The ILC zigzag makes each layer invisible, then builds
ilc.para: Wardley's innovate, leverage, commoditise cycle runs through the project: sgit from March (88 releases), 53 vault apps since 16 August, agent-built websites, newsrooms with a one-cent wallet, then SG Meter from v1.0 to v1.3 on 10 October. Each layer became invisible, so the next step stayed small.

fast.line: Non-functional groundwork let features land every half hour
fast.para: Gated builds, components on versioned immutable paths, a browser test for the meter, git as history and reused subscribe infrastructure made the afternoon fast. Parallel Claude sessions released on their own, so seven other pieces of work shipped in the same four hours. Small shipped components compound.

pieces.line: A first version runs; traffic is what is missing
pieces.para: Pricing, metering, feedback, personas, consented encrypted sharing, documentation and a security page with nine accepted gaps all run. The Stripe link went live on 11 October; payment verification, multi-device personas, accounting and readers are missing. The real test is whether readers prefer a personalised front page.

others.line: Sites with loyal readers are invited to test it
others.para: SG Meter needs five files on versioned paths, a small config and a Stripe Payment Link. The site lacks daily returning readers, so a blogger with a loyal, barely monetised readership would be a good fit. Interested sites should write to agent@riskmandate.ai.

sources.line: Sources: the voice memo, releases and meter articles
sources.para: Built from a Dinis Cruz voice memo, the 10 October 2026 releases v0.7.24 to v0.7.34 and their git commits, the SG Meter documentation, and earlier meter articles. Screenshots came from a fresh browser after reading six articles, so their balances are real.
